1. Statutory framework and how the system works  

Under the SSI scheme in 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c), Congress did three important things:

- It adopted **retrospective monthly accounting (RMA)** as the general rule: benefits in month M are based on income in month M−2.  
- It carved out a **special rule for the first (and optionally second) month** of eligibility in § 1382(c)(2)(A), where the agency does *not* use RMA but instead looks to “the income, resources, and other relevant circumstances” of those initial months.  
- In § 1382(c)(5), it created an **express special rule for certain enumerated income items**, which “shall be taken into account only for the month in which received.”

The agency’s “transitional computation cycle” is its way of implementing this:  
- Month 1 (and if the Secretary chooses, Month 2): prospective/actual-month computation under § 1382(c)(2)(A).  
- By Month 3, the statute requires going back to RMA (the two‑month look‑back). That will necessarily “pull in” whatever income existed two months prior, including one‑time payments received in Month 1.

The Carter Class objects that this allows the same one‑time payment to depress benefits in multiple months (Month 1 prospectively, plus later months through RMA), which they characterize as an unfair “triple deduction.”

2. Textual analysis of § 1382(c)(2)(A)  

Section 1382(c)(2)(A) provides (in substance) that for the first month in which a person is entitled, the agency shall compute the benefit:

> “on the basis of the income, resources, and other relevant circumstances in such month (and, at the option of the Secretary, in the succeeding month)…”

Key points:

- The provision is **about which information to use in those particular months**, not about how that income may or may not be used in the RMA regime that resumes later.
- The Carter Class argument is: because Congress told the Secretary to consider “other relevant circumstances” in the first month, that requires the agency to recognize the **nonrecurring nature** of the payment and to ensure it is not allowed to reduce later months’ benefits again.

The difficulty with that reading is:

- The text does **not** say that income considered under § 1382(c)(2)(A) “shall not thereafter be taken into account” or “shall be counted only once.”  
- “Other relevant circumstances” is naturally read as **what affects the amount of benefits in the initial month(s)**—e.g., whether the person is institutionalized, what their living arrangements are, whether their resources exceed limits—not as a prohibition on how RMA will operate later.
- If Congress meant to create a “single-use” rule for all nonrecurring income received in the first month, it could easily have used the same explicit “only for the month in which received” phrasing it used elsewhere in this very subsection (see § 1382(c)(5)).

So § 1382(c)(2)(A) comfortably supports the Secretary’s current practice:  
- The gate‑release payment **is** considered in the first month’s calculation as part of “income … and other relevant circumstances.”  
- The statute then tells the agency to apply the RMA framework thereafter; it never says income from Month 1 is *forbidden* to be used in those later RMA calculations.

3. Textual analysis of § 1382(c)(5)  

Section 1382(c)(5) specifically addresses how certain categories of income are treated over time. Without needing the exact list, the important structural point is:

- Congress **expressly identified particular kinds of income that “shall be taken into account only for the month in which [they are] received.”**
- It did **not** put gate‑release payments, or nonrecurring payments generally, into that category.

This directly undermines the Carter Class’s position. Their rule would in effect say:

> Any one‑time, nonrecurring payment received in the first month gets the same treatment Congress gave to the enumerated items in § 1382(c)(5): it can affect only that month and not later months.

But Congress, when it wanted one‑month‑only treatment, **wrote it down explicitly** and did so narrowly. The familiar interpretive principle (expressio unius) applies strongly here:

- When Congress **enumerates** some types of income that “shall be taken into account only for the month in which received,” it implies that **other income is not so limited**.
- A court adopting the Carter Class’s reading would effectively be **adding a new category** to § 1382(c)(5) (all one‑time first‑month payments) that Congress itself did not include.

A court that takes statutory text and structure seriously will be very hesitant to do that, especially in a detailed benefits statute where Congress has clearly attended to month‑by‑month treatment in a granular way.

4. Is the Secretary “triple counting” the same income?  

The Carter Class’s “triple deduction” framing is rhetorically powerful but analytically misleading.

Under RMA:

- Income is **assigned to, and affects, the month in which it is received** for accounting purposes.
- That month’s income then becomes the reference for **later months** under the look‑back rule.

So if someone receives a one‑time payment in Month 1:

- It properly reduces Month 1’s benefit under § 1382(c)(2)(A) (using actual income that month).
- When Month 3 is computed using RMA, the statute directs SSA to look back to the income in Month 1. That’s not “charging” the same dollar twice; it is applying the standard, congressionally prescribed two‑month look‑back formula.

It is the **nature of RMA** that irregular or nonrecurring spikes in income can affect multiple future months. That is not special to gate‑release payments or to newly eligible beneficiaries; it is how the system works for everyone.

Nothing in § 1382(c)(2)(A) says that income treated under the first‑month rule loses its status as “income received in that month” for RMA purposes, and nothing in § 1382(c)(5) reclassifies nonrecurring first‑month payments as “one‑month‑only” income.

5. Purposive and fairness arguments  

The Carter Class makes substantial equitable points:

- SSI is a **supplemental** program aimed at maintaining a minimal standard of living. People just leaving detention are especially vulnerable.  
- Letting a small gate‑release payment depress benefits over several months may seem harsh and arguably undermines the program’s remedial purpose.  
- The phrase “other relevant circumstances” in § 1382(c)(2)(A) could be read to include the nonrecurring nature of the payment, supporting a one‑month‑only effect as more consistent with fairness.

Courts sometimes use pro‑beneficiary canons in social welfare statutes, but those canons normally come into play **only where the text is genuinely ambiguous**. Here, two features make it difficult to say there is such ambiguity:

1. Congress already addressed the precise question of **whether certain income counts only once or can affect multiple months**—and chose to limit that protection to specific, enumerated items in § 1382(c)(5).  
2. § 1382(c)(2)(A) is naturally read as a **timing rule for what information is used in Month 1 (and perhaps Month 2)**, not as a hidden, categorical restriction on how the RMA formula may use that month’s income going forward.

In other words, to reach the Carter Class’s reading, the court would need to infer:

- A broad, unstated “single‑count” rule for nonrecurring first‑month income from the phrase “other relevant circumstances,” and  
- Ignore the way Congress explicitly and narrowly wrote single‑month‑only rules in § 1382(c)(5).

That is a large step beyond what traditional statutory interpretation allows, even in remedial statutes.

6. Deference and agency implementation  

After the Supreme Court’s recent retreat from Chevron‑style mandatory deference, a court does not simply “automatically” uphold any reasonable agency reading. But here that point is almost secondary, because:

- The **best reading of the statute on its own terms** already supports the Secretary: nothing prohibits later RMA use of first‑month income, and § 1382(c)(5) affirmatively suggests Congress did *not* intend a broad one‑month‑only rule for nonrecurring payments.
- The agency’s transitional computation cycle is a **straightforward implementation** of Congress’s choice of RMA, coupled with the special initial‑month rule. It is not an attempt to evade or rewrite the statute.

Even considered under a more modest Skidmore standard (persuasiveness rather than deference), the agency’s interpretation is **coherent, textually grounded, and consistent with the structure and administrative goals** (accuracy and prevention of overpayments) that Congress embedded in the RMA framework.

7. Bottom line  

The Carter Class has strong policy and fairness concerns, and Congress might reasonably decide to amend the statute to ensure one‑time gate‑release payments do not depress several months of post‑release benefits. But under the statute as written:

- § 1382(c)(2)(A) does not bar later RMA use of first‑month income; it only prescribes how to calculate the first (and optionally second) month.  
- § 1382(c)(5) shows that when Congress wants income to count only once, it says so expressly; it has not said so for gate‑release payments or nonrecurring income generally.  
- The Secretary’s policy fits the text, the structure, and the logic of RMA; the Carter Class’s proposed “single-count” rule would effectively rewrite § 1382(c)(5) by adding a new category that Congress chose not to include.

On balance, a U.S. court applying ordinary principles of statutory interpretation should uphold the Secretary’s approach and reject the Carter Class’s challenge.

1. **Legal framework**

- Refugee status and humanitarian protection turn on whether there is a **“reasonable degree of likelihood”** (or “real risk”) that, if returned, Mr. Ho would face:
  - persecution for a Refugee Convention reason, or
  - serious harm contrary to Article 3 ECHR / humanitarian protection.
- Under **s.8 Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004**, specified behaviours (e.g. late claims) must be treated as **damaging to credibility**, though not automatically fatal.
- Where the feared harm is from **non‑state actors**, Mr. Ho must show the **Vietnamese state is unable or unwilling** to provide him with a “sufficiency of protection”, or that effective internal relocation is not reasonable.

2. **Credibility and the medical evidence**

- The core of Mr. Ho’s account is that:
  - powerful individuals linked to local structures extorted annual bribes,
  - this related to his military exemption,
  - he was assaulted when he could not pay,
  - he left Vietnam in fear.
- The **medical reports** from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital:
  - provide some **objective evidence of injuries** consistent with assaults;
  - but, on his own case, he **gave false explanations** to clinicians about how those injuries occurred.
- In an English tribunal, that feature is critical: where the only **independent corroboration** (the medical notes) conflicts with the later asylum narrative, the reports become **neutral at best** on cause and perpetrator. They show he was injured; they do not reliably corroborate *why* or *by whom*.
- His explanation—that he feared retaliation and so lied to medical staff—is **plausible in the abstract**, but the tribunal must weigh:
  - the absence of any mention of extortion or politically tinged conflict in the contemporaneous records;
  - the fact that these are **the only objective documents** tying to the alleged past persecution.
- Given that his whole narrative about persecution, corruption, and link to military exemption ultimately rests on **his oral account**, the tribunal is entitled, and likely, to place **limited corroborative weight** on the medical reports.

3. **Military exemption and the extortion narrative**

- Official documents relied on by the Secretary of State confirm that, by reason of his father’s martyr status, Mr. Ho **did not, in law, face military service**.
- It is not impossible that corrupt actors could still exploit him; however, for his account to be accepted:
  - the tribunal would expect **some concrete evidence** or at least a coherent explanation of how such extortions operated despite clear legal exemption;
  - the absence of any documentary trace of demands, payments, or related complaints is a significant weakness.
- Faced with:
  - clear, reliable official evidence of exempt status, and
  - no tangible support for the alleged bribe‑demand system,
  the tribunal is likely to find that **this central aspect of his story lacks sufficient credibility**.

4. **Failure to seek protection and sufficiency of protection**

- For non‑state persecution, Mr. Ho must show that **state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming**.
- Here:
  - He **never sought assistance** from any Vietnamese authority.
  - He relies on a general assertion that the extortionists were “embedded in local power structures” and that recourse to official channels would be futile or dangerous.
- English asylum jurisprudence requires more than generalized claims of corruption. Vietnam is not treated as a failed state; while corruption exists, there is no general country guidance that **effective protection is unavailable** for victims of local criminality or abuse.
- Without:
  - past attempts to obtain protection,
  - evidence of specific collusion (names, ranks, documented interactions),
  his case on the **unavailability of state protection is speculative**.
- A tribunal is therefore likely to find:
  - either there is **a sufficiency of protection** in Vietnam, or
  - any risk is localised and **internal relocation** within Vietnam would be both safe and reasonable.

5. **Late asylum claim and s.8 2004 Act**

- Mr. Ho only claimed asylum **after** deportation action was initiated, following his serious criminal conviction in the UK.
- Under **s.8**, that late claim must be treated as **damaging his credibility**. It does not automatically defeat the claim, but it is a substantial adverse factor.
- His explanations—fear for his family, confusion about procedures, and precarious status—are possible, but contrasted with:
  - his ability to navigate employment abroad,
  - his engagement in serious organised criminality,
  a tribunal is unlikely to accept that he was too confused or fearful to raise protection concerns earlier.
- Given the centrality of timing in s.8 analysis, and in light of an already weakly corroborated narrative, the **late, reactive nature** of the claim will significantly reinforce the Secretary of State’s position.

6. **Convention reason / humanitarian protection**

- Even if his account of extortion were accepted at a low standard of proof, there are further difficulties:
  - It is not clearly shown that the harm arises **“for reasons of”** a Convention ground (race, religion, nationality, political opinion, PSG). The motive appears primarily **financial** (extortion), not punishment for political or other protected characteristics.
  - An argument of imputed political opinion (opposition to corrupt officials) is conceivable but not well‑developed on the facts provided.
- For **humanitarian protection / Article 3**, he must still show a real risk of serious harm without adequate state protection. For reasons above (credibility and likely sufficiency of protection), that threshold is also **not reached**.

7. **Overall assessment**

- Applying the “reasonable degree of likelihood” standard to:
  - the **limited corroborative value** of the medical reports,
  - the **implausibility and undocumented nature** of the extortion scheme in light of his legal exemption,
  - his **complete failure to seek protection** from Vietnamese authorities,
  - and the **significant negative credibility impact** of his late, post‑deportation asylum claim under s.8,
- an English tribunal is likely to find that Mr. Ho has **not discharged the burden** of demonstrating a real risk of persecution or serious harm on return.
- His account, taken cumulatively, falls **below the low standard of proof** once the adverse credibility findings mandated by the 2004 Act are weighed against the weak corroboration and the availability of state protection.

On that basis, the appeal should be dismissed and the Secretary of State’s decision upheld.

Under the STAA, a driver prevails only if he shows (1) protected activity; (2) adverse action; (3) the employer knew of the protected activity; and (4) the protected activity was a contributing factor in the adverse action. The employer can avoid liability by clear and convincing evidence it would have taken the same action absent the protected conduct. 49 U.S.C. § 31105 (successor to 49 U.S.C. app. §§ 2301‑2305).

There are two possible categories of protected activity here:

1. **Refusal to operate due to unsafe conditions (fatigue)** – grounded in 49 C.F.R. § 392.3.  
2. **Complaints or objections about safety or regulatory compliance** – including internal complaints.

I’ll address each.

---

### 1. Was Jackson’s conduct a protected “refusal to operate” due to fatigue?

49 C.F.R. § 392.3 prohibits a driver from operating when his “ability or alertness is so impaired, or so likely to become impaired, through fatigue … as to make it unsafe” and prohibits a carrier from requiring or permitting such operation. Under the STAA, a driver is protected when he **refuses** to operate because doing so would violate this rule or would be unsafe.

Key facts:

- Jackson **accepted all dispatches**; he did not decline any assignment or tell the company “I cannot take this run because I am too fatigued.”  
- On the Faircreek run, he left late (partly due to equipment repairs) after having been awake many hours and then pulled over mid‑trip to sleep because he felt fatigued.  
- On the Everton runs, his lateness was due in part to an extra coffee break and time spent unloading his personal belongings, as well as traffic, weather, and an accident.

Two questions matter:

**(a) Does stopping en route to rest qualify as a “refusal to operate”?**  
Courts and the DOL have treated a mid‑trip decision to stop driving based on fatigue as potentially within the scope of a “refusal,” because it is a decision not to continue operating under unsafe conditions. On these facts, Jackson’s decision to pull over and sleep when he felt fatigued is the kind of conduct § 392.3 is designed to encourage.

But STAA protection does not automatically mean **all consequences of being late** are illegal. The driver must show that the employer’s adverse action was **because** of that protected refusal, not merely because of chronic performance issues.

**(b) What was Green Logistics actually disciplining?**  
The record shows:

- The company had previously counseled Jackson multiple times for delayed freight before these particular runs.  
- Green Logistics had structured options (slide time, grace periods, ability to choose days off) to avoid fatigue. Jackson did not use them.  
- The disciplinary notices reference **“delayed freight”** and “delaying freight and equipment”; later letters and the suspension follow repeated late arrivals, some due to plainly non‑safety reasons (extra coffee break, extra time unloading personal belongings).

On the Faircreek trip, Jackson’s late arrival stemmed from a mix of factors: late departure (repairs and prior wakefulness) and his fatigue stop. On the Everton trips, the non‑safety factors (personal coffee break; unloading personal items) loom larger.

Taken together, the pattern indicates Green Logistics was focused on his overall, recurrent **tardiness and non‑adherence to dispatch expectations**, not on punishing him for a safety‑motivated refusal. In particular:

- There is no indication his supervisors objected to a driver stopping when too tired per se; indeed, the company’s anti‑fatigue policies cut the other way.  
- Jackson himself apparently believed he was free to operate at his own pace and take additional breaks; the company, by contrast, emphasized meeting delivery schedules. The conflict is thus about productivity and timeliness, not safety.

Even if Jackson’s mid‑trip rest was a technically protected “refusal,” Green Logistics has a strong “same‑action” defense: its discipline was grounded in a **documented pattern of late deliveries**, exacerbated by non‑safety‑related conduct (personal breaks, personal unloading), and not uniquely or primarily tied to the one fatigue stop. On this record, it is difficult for Jackson to show that his protected decision to rest was a contributing factor in the suspension and disciplinary letters as opposed to the pervasive lateness problems.

---

### 2. Were Jackson’s “objections” protected safety complaints?

STAA also protects a driver who:

- “files a complaint or begins a proceeding” about a violation of commercial vehicle safety regulations, or  
- “is about to file” such a complaint, or  
- “testifies” or cooperates in such a proceeding.

Informal, internal complaints about **safety or regulatory noncompliance** can qualify, but mere disagreement with routine personnel actions does not.

Here, the record describes Jackson as:

- “voicing concerns about the contents of his employment file” and  
- “objecting to disciplinary letters.”

There is no clear evidence that these objections explicitly raised **safety** or regulatory concerns. If Jackson simply said, in substance, “I don’t agree with these warnings” or “this makes my record look bad,” that is not protected activity. To be protected, he would have needed to tie his objections to compliance with 49 C.F.R. § 392.3 or other DOT safety rules (e.g., “You are disciplining me for obeying the fatigue rule; that’s illegal”).

The problem for Jackson is that the record, as stated, characterizes his objections as concerning his **employment record**, not as assertions that Green Logistics was violating federal safety regulations or punishing him for obeying those regulations. On these facts, a court is likely to find:

- His internal objections were not sufficiently framed as safety or regulatory complaints to fall within the STAA;  
- The actual, formal STAA complaint he filed was with DOL **after** the discipline, and there is no alleged adverse action that followed that filing.

Accordingly, his “objections” do not appear to be independently protected activity.

---

### 3. Causation and pretext

Even assuming some protected activity (the fatigue‑based rest), Jackson still must show that such activity **contributed** to the discipline. Then Green Logistics can avoid liability by clear and convincing evidence that it would have imposed the same discipline absent the protected conduct.

The employer’s defense is strong on the undisputed facts:

- Repeated, prior counseling for delayed freight before the trips at issue;  
- Multiple written notices and a suspension aligned with a **pattern** of late arrivals, not a one‑off fatigue event;  
- Non‑safety contributors to delay (extra coffee break, extended unloading of personal belongings) that the company reasonably viewed as unacceptable;  
- Well‑documented business need for timely deliveries and no evidence of hostility to safety‑based shutdowns.

A court applying the STAA burden‑shifting framework would likely conclude:

- Jackson has at best a thin prima facie case (limited protected activity; weak evidence that this was the reason for discipline).  
- Green Logistics has ample, non‑pretextual, performance‑based reasons for the discipline and can convincingly show it would have reacted the same way even if his mid‑trip rest were treated as wholly protected.

Crucially, the STAA does not immunize a driver from consequences of poor performance simply because some portion of a trip’s delay relates to a safety stop. The law prevents an employer from punishing a driver **for** refusing to drive unsafely; it does not require the employer to ignore a broader history of chronic tardiness and clearly non‑safety‑related delays.

---

### 4. Conclusion

Given the totality of the facts and the structure of the STAA:

- Jackson’s mid‑journey fatigue stop may fall within the ambit of safety‑motivated conduct that the law encourages.  
- However, the disciplinary letters and suspension are most credibly explained by his longstanding pattern of late deliveries and unprotected behavior (extra personal breaks, personal unloading, disregard of the company’s dispatch expectations), not by any protected refusal or complaint.  
- His objections to the disciplinary letters, as described, are not clearly safety complaints and thus are not protected activity.  
- Green Logistics can show by clear and convincing evidence that it would have imposed the same discipline regardless of any protected rest stop.

On these facts, a U.S. court applying the STAA and related regulations should find in favor of the employer.

1. **Statutory structure and what’s actually at issue**

The provisions in play are part of the SSI “retrospective monthly accounting” (RMA) system in 42 U.S.C. § 1382(c).

- **§ 1382(c)(1)** (in substance): For ongoing recipients, the “benefit for a month” is computed based on **income received in the second month prior** (the M–2 rule).
- **§ 1382(c)(2)(A)**: Creates an **exception for the first month (and, at the Secretary’s option, the second month)** of eligibility after a period of ineligibility. For those months the benefit is computed:
  - “on the basis of the income, resources, and other relevant circumstances in such month.”
  - and **“without regard”** to the RMA rule in § 1382(c)(1).
- **§ 1382(c)(5)**: For **specific, enumerated categories of payments**, Congress directs that such payments are to be **“counted only for the month in which received”** (or equivalent language) and not carried forward into later months’ computations.

The Carter Class’s concrete complaint is that a **one-time gate release payment**, received in the first month after regaining eligibility, reduced benefits in **three months**:
- once when month 1 was computed “prospectively” on the basis of income in that month,  
- again in the transitional second month, and  
- yet again when RMA resumed and month 3’s benefit was computed on the basis of month 1 income (the M–2 rule).

So the question is not whether the payment can be counted at all; it’s whether the **same nonrecurring payment may lawfully affect multiple months of benefits**, or must be confined to a single month’s calculation.

---

2. **Parsing § 1382(c)(2)(A): what does it actually command?**

The critical statutory phrase is that in the first (and optional second) month, the benefit:

> “shall be computed … on the basis of the income, resources, and other relevant circumstances in such month.”

Key points:

- Grammatically, this text governs **how benefits for that particular month** must be computed.
- It **displaces the usual M–2 rule** (§ 1382(c)(1)) *for that month’s* computation—by requiring the agency to look at the recipient’s actual income and circumstances in that same month, not at income two months earlier.
- Nothing in the text of § 1382(c)(2)(A) speaks to **how income from that month may or may not be used when computing later months** once the system reverts to RMA.

The Carter Class’s argument is that “other relevant circumstances in such month” must include the fact that the gate payment is **nonrecurring**, and that recognizing this “relevant circumstance” implicitly forbids allowing that income to be used again in later RMA-based months.

But textually:

- “Other relevant circumstances in such month” is **tethered to the computation for that month**. It requires a realistic, contemporaneous determination of the first month’s benefit, taking into account actual conditions (e.g., a change in disability, marriage, residence, and—plausibly—whether income is recurring or not).
- It does **not** purport to be a global rule that any income whose nonrecurring nature is “relevant” in month 1 **may never be reflected again** when that month’s income naturally appears in the M–2 formula for month 3.

If Congress had meant to prohibit subsequent RMA use of that income, it could easily have said, for example, that income used in the first (and second) month “shall not be taken into account in determining benefits for any other month.” It did not.

So, on its face, § 1382(c)(2)(A):

- **Requires** a month‑specific computation for month 1 (and optionally month 2),
- **Does not address at all** whether the same month’s income may later appear in the RMA computation for month 3 and beyond.

That silence is important when we turn to § 1382(c)(5).

---

3. **Role of § 1382(c)(5): express treatment of “one‑month only” income**

Section 1382(c)(5) (as described) explicitly provides that **certain identified categories of payments** “shall be counted only for the month in which received.”

Two consequences follow:

1. Congress clearly understood that **some income can be nonrecurring** and decided to **isolate those specific categories** for special “one‑month only” treatment.
2. By doing so, Congress showed it knows how to write a rule that **prevents income from affecting more than one month** of benefits when it wishes.

Under standard interpretive canons:

- **Expressio unius est exclusio alterius** (the expression of one thing implies the exclusion of others) fits well here. Where Congress has:
  - created a general RMA rule, and  
  - then carved out specific categories of income that may **only** be counted once,
  
  the natural inference is that **income not in those categories is subject to the normal accounting rules, even if nonrecurring**.

The Carter Class resists that inference by saying § 1382(c)(5) is merely a “concrete instantiation” of a broader principle implicit in § 1382(c)(2)(A). But that re-describes, rather than explains, the statutory structure. If a broad, across‑the‑board rule already existed—i.e., that any nonrecurring income must be confined to one month—there would be little reason for Congress to go on and separately specify one‑month counting for listed payment types. Section 1382(c)(5) functions far more naturally as an **exception to the baseline RMA regime**, not as a redundant affirmation of an already implicit general rule.

Read together, the provisions point in this direction:

- **Baseline**: All income, including nonrecurring income, fits into the RMA machinery—meaning income received in month N may affect benefits for month N and (through M–2 accounting) for subsequent months.
- **Exception for initial month(s)**: For month 1 (and optionally month 2), the agency must compute on actual income and circumstances “in such month” instead of applying a backward‑looking formula. This is about how to determine *those months’* benefits.
- **Special one‑month-only categories** (§ 1382(c)(5)): Certain **specified** types of payments, and only those, are insulated from having multi‑month consequences.

On this reading, the Secretary’s treatment of Carter’s gate release payment as affecting multiple months is **exactly what the structure presupposes**, unless the payment falls into a § 1382(c)(5) category (and the facts as framed assume it does not).

---

4. **The “triple deduction” objection and the concept of income “received in” a month**

It is intuitive to say that “the same dollar” is being deducted three times, and that this therefore misconceives what it means for income to be “received in” a month.

But in an RMA system, that’s not what is happening as a matter of statutory mechanics:

- In month 1, Carter **actually receives** the gate payment; his benefit for month 1 is computed “on the basis of the income … in such month.” So the payment legitimately reduces **month 1** benefits.
- In month 3, when RMA is active, the statute directs that the **benefit for month 3** is computed “on the basis of income … received in the second month preceding such month”—i.e., the income actually received in month 1.
- The statute is not **counting the gate payment as if newly received in month 3**; it is simply *using the fact that he received that income in month 1* as the basis for the month 3 calculation.

The “double” or “triple” impact flows from the combination of:

- (a) a special rule for how to compute month‑1 (and possibly month‑2) benefits, and  
- (b) the neutral, general RMA instruction to use month‑1 income again in computing month‑3 benefits.

Nothing in the text bars that interaction. Indeed, it is the **expected byproduct** of having both (a) and (b) on the books at once. To convert “relevant circumstances in such month” into an implied prohibition on month‑1 income ever influencing later months is to add additional words to the statute that Congress did not write.

---

5. **Purpose, fairness, and the social‑welfare canon**

The Carter Class invokes two broader themes:

1. **Purpose**: The initial‑month exception is said to be a hardship‑preventing measure; allowing a triple reduction turns that protection into a penalty.
2. **Social‑welfare canon**: Ambiguities in social‑welfare statutes are often said to be resolved in favor of beneficiaries.

On purpose:

- It is plausible that § 1382(c)(2)(A) was enacted to avoid **gaps or distortions** at the point where people first come (or return) onto the rolls, by basing initial benefits on their **actual current circumstances** rather than outdated income data.
- But that purpose is fully served by enforcing the statute as written: month‑1 (and possibly month‑2) benefits must reflect reality “in such month” and not hypothetical or stale income.
- The statute **does not speak** to whether Congress also sought to protect beneficiaries from any multi‑month consequences of income in that first month. That protective gloss is **policy‑driven**, not text‑driven.

On the social‑welfare canon:

- Modern Supreme Court practice gives **primacy to text and structure**. A “liberal construction” or pro‑beneficiary canon cannot override clear statutory direction.
- The relevant question is whether the statute is genuinely **ambiguous** on the key issue (multi‑month use of month‑1 income). For the reasons above, the structure—especially the presence of § 1382(c)(5)—strongly suggests that **Congress contemplated some multi‑month effects of nonrecurring income** and chose to limit them only for certain specified payments.
- At most, any ambiguity is slight, and it is countered by the more specific design choices (enumerated one‑month‑only categories; silence otherwise) that support the Secretary’s view.

Thus, while fairness concerns are real, the statutory text does not plausibly contain the broad, anti‑“cascade” rule the Carter Class seeks.

---

6. **Agency interpretation and administrative workability (post‑Chevron context)**

Even assuming Chevron deference is no longer controlling, a court still looks at agency interpretations under something like **Skidmore**—considering their thoroughness, longevity, and consistency, and the fit with the statute.

Here:

- The Secretary’s “transitional computation cycle” rules are detailed, longstanding, and directly tied to implementing RMA in a way that maintains **administrative regularity and predictability**.
- The agency has not invented some ad hoc penalty; it is applying **the same RMA logic to all income**, subject only to those explicit statutory exceptions (§ 1382(c)(5)).
- From a systems perspective, limiting all nonrecurring income to a single month (beyond the specified categories) would require complex exception‑layering and would depart from RMA’s **simple, mechanical reliance on actual prior‑month income**.

Courts are not obliged to defer blindly, but where the **better textual reading already aligns** with the agency’s consistent practice and preserves administrative coherency, there is no warrant to discard it.

---

7. **Bottom line**

- Section 1382(c)(2)(A) governs **how** to calculate benefits **for the first (and possibly second) month**—by reference to “income … and other relevant circumstances in such month.” It does **not** address whether that month’s income may later be used, via RMA, in computing later months.
- Section 1382(c)(5) shows that when Congress wants certain nonrecurring payments to be **“counted only for the month in which received,”** it says so expressly and does so for **specific categories**, implying that other income is left to the general RMA rules.
- Reading the provisions together, and giving effect to both the initial‑month exception and the explicit one‑month‑only categories, the more coherent interpretation is that **Carter’s gate release payment can lawfully affect multiple months’ benefits** under the transitional/RMA scheme.
- The Carter Class’s fairness concerns are real, but they seek a limitation that the statute does not itself impose. Any adjustment to avoid multi‑month impact of all nonrecurring income is better viewed as a **legislative** choice, not a judicial re‑writing of the existing text.

Accordingly, on the law as written, the **Secretary’s position should prevail.**

A court applying the Federal Arbitration Act (FAA) and ordinary contract principles should deny Jon Davidson’s motion to compel arbitration and hold that Harper Investors need not arbitrate with him.

---

### 1. Governing legal framework

1. Under the FAA, arbitration is “a matter of contract.” Courts must:
   - Enforce agreements to arbitrate **according to their terms**, and  
   - Use **state contract law** to decide whether a nonsignatory may enforce an arbitration clause (Arthur Andersen LLP v. Carlisle; Granite Rock Co. v. Teamsters).

2. As a nonsignatory, Davidson has **no presumptive right** to compel arbitration. He must fit within a recognized contract‑law theory that allows a nonsignatory to enforce an arbitration agreement, such as:
   - Assumption or assignment,
   - Agency,
   - Third‑party beneficiary status,
   - Successor in interest (e.g., merger),
   - Equitable estoppel (direct‑benefit or “intertwined claims” variants).

If none of these applies, the FAA’s general “policy favoring arbitration” cannot create an arbitration right that the contract itself does not supply.

---

### 2. The arbitration clause and what it actually covers

The clause here is broad: disputes “arising out of or relating to” the agreement between Harper Investors and Gold Reserve & Lending are to be arbitrated.

That breadth matters for **which disputes between contracting parties** must go to arbitration. It does **not** answer the logically prior question: *who* is entitled to enforce the clause. Even a very broad clause does not, standing alone, extend arbitration rights to every later‑involved person related to the signatory.

So the question is not whether the subject matter of the claims “relates to” the agreement (many of Harper’s claims do), but whether Davidson as an individual has any legal basis, under contract law, to invoke the clause.

---

### 3. The main theories a court would consider

#### A. Assignment or assumption of Gold Reserve’s contractual rights

There is no indication that:

- Gold Reserve assigned its rights under the Harper contract to Davidson personally, or  
- Davidson expressly assumed Gold Reserve’s contractual position in that agreement.

He acquired Gold Reserve “through an entity called National Freight Consolidated” and served as owner/officer/director. Under well‑established principles (exemplified by Thomson–CSF v. American Arbitration Ass’n and similar cases), **acquiring a corporation’s stock or control does not automatically assign that corporation’s contracts to the owner personally**. The separate corporate form continues to exist; the corporation—not its shareholders, not its officers—remains the contractual party.

Without a formal assignment, assumption agreement, or statutory merger putting Davidson individually in Gold Reserve’s shoes, he has no direct contractual standing to invoke the clause in his own name.

#### B. Third‑party beneficiary

To be an intended third‑party beneficiary, the contract must clearly indicate that the contracting parties **intended to confer enforceable rights** on that nonparty.

- There is no evidence that the Harper–Gold Reserve agreement states or implies that present or future owners, officers, or consultants of Gold Reserve can compel arbitration in their personal capacities.
- At most, Davidson is a **foreseeable incidental beneficiary** of Gold Reserve’s business relationships; that is not enough to give him contract rights.

So third‑party‑beneficiary status is not available.

#### C. Agency and officer status

Courts sometimes allow a nonsignatory employee or agent of a signatory to compel arbitration where:

1. The plaintiff’s claims against the agent arise from the agent’s conduct **within the scope of the relationship created by the contract**, and  
2. The claims against the agent are **inseparable** from claims against the principal signatory based on the same agreement.

Examples: broker‑employees relying on a customer’s brokerage agreement; corporate officers sued for misrepresentations made in executing a contract that contains the clause.

Here, the facts cut against extending that line of cases to Davidson:

- Davidson’s alleged wrongful acts **go beyond merely carrying out Gold Reserve’s contractual obligations**. Harper alleges that he:
  - Operated under *separate* entities (Universal Business Services; Fund Restoration Alliance; Tax Support Circle),  
  - Initiated **new, distinct solicitations** of funds, and  
  - Urged investors not to sue while implying he was “helping” them, all post‑contract.

Those are not just acts of an officer executing the existing investment contract; they are alleged **independent frauds and schemes**, undertaken through later‑formed entities with their own identities and purposes.

- Harper is seeking to hold Davidson **personally liable** not just as an agent carrying out Gold Reserve’s contract, but as the designer and operator of additional, later schemes.

In the agency‑cases that do allow employees/officers to compel arbitration, the claims are essentially that the agents did **on behalf of the corporation** the very things the contract covers. Here, by contrast, Harper’s claims involve **new conduct, new entities, and new solicitations**, even if they are connected to the original tax shelter background.

Thus, Davidson’s status as an owner/officer/director does not, without more, entitle him to enforce the clause.

#### D. Successor‑in‑interest / corporate acquisition

Davidson acquired Gold Reserve through National Freight Consolidated, but the facts don’t state that:

- Gold Reserve was merged out of existence into Davidson or into National Freight, or  
- There was a transaction making Davidson personally the legal successor of Gold Reserve’s rights and obligations under the Harper contract.

As in Thomson–CSF and similar decisions, a **share purchase or acquisition of corporate control** is not equivalent to a merger that transfers contractual status. The corporation remains a distinct legal person.

Absent veil‑piercing (which Harper is not seeking here) or a formal merger, Davidson is **not** Gold Reserve for purposes of enforcing the contract; he is at most its indirect owner.

#### E. Equitable estoppel

There are two main estoppel theories courts use to let a nonsignatory enforce arbitration:

1. **Direct‑benefit estoppel:** the signatory directly exploits the benefits of the contract (not merely its background) and then tries to avoid its arbitration clause; or

2. **Intertwined‑claims estoppel:** the signatory’s claims against the nonsignatory are so intimately founded on and intertwined with the contract containing the arbitration clause that it would be inequitable to allow the signatory to rely on the contract substantively while disavowing its arbitration provision.

Applied here:

**1. Direct‑benefit estoppel**

Harper is not suing to enforce the Harper–Gold Reserve contract against Davidson. Their core theory is that Davidson ran a tax shelter fraud and subsequent “restoration” schemes through entities separate from Gold Reserve and misled investors about pursuing claims.

Harper does not seek to hold Davidson liable on a contractual promise **in the Harper–Gold Reserve agreement**. Its claims rely on tort and statutory duties (fraud, misrepresentation, possibly RICO or similar claims) that exist independent of the contract.

So Harper is not “accepting the benefits” of that contract as to Davidson while repudiating its burdens; direct‑benefit estoppel does not apply.

**2. Intertwined‑claims estoppel**

Some of Harper’s allegations likely relate to the original container leasing/tax shelter investments sold under the Gold Reserve contracts. But courts are careful here: the fact that a tort claim **arises in the factual context of a contract** is not enough for estoppel. The question is whether the plaintiff’s claims **against the nonsignatory** are “intertwined” in the sense that the plaintiff must rely on the contract’s terms or assert violations of duties created by that contract.

- Harper’s claims against Davidson concern fraudulent inducements, solicitations, and post‑investment schemes under Universal Business Services, Fund Restoration Alliance, and Tax Support Circle. Those alleged wrongs can be pleaded and proven **without the court ever needing to interpret or enforce any specific term of the Harper–Gold Reserve contract**.
- The connection is largely chronological and factual: the investors’ relationship with Davidson arose because of the original tax shelter. But under decisions like Thomson–CSF, Comer v. Micor, and Kramer v. Toyota (among others), that level of connection is not enough; “but‑for” factual relation to a contract does not automatically make the claims sufficiently “intertwined” to compel estoppel‑based arbitration with a nonsignatory.

In short, Harper does not seek to both (a) hold Davidson liable under the contract and (b) avoid the arbitration clause in that same contract. Instead, it sues him for **separate, post‑contract misconduct**. That is precisely the situation where courts typically *decline* to apply equitable estoppel in favor of nonsignatories.

---

### 4. The federal “policy favoring arbitration” does not bridge this gap

Davidson emphasizes the FAA’s “strong federal policy favoring arbitration” and the broad language “arising out of or relating to.” But the Supreme Court has repeatedly made two limiting points:

1. The federal policy **“is at bottom a policy guaranteeing the enforcement of private contractual arrangements”**—not a policy of creating arbitration rights where none were agreed to.
2. Courts must decide **“whether the parties agreed to arbitrate”** before applying any presumption in favor of arbitration, and they may not reorder basic state contract rules to expand who is bound or benefitted by arbitration clauses (see, e.g., Granite Rock; Stolt‑Nielsen; Lamps Plus).

Here, Harper never agreed to arbitrate disputes with Jon Davidson personally or with his later‑formed entities. Without any contract‑law basis to treat Davidson as a party, assignee, intended beneficiary, successor, or estoppel‑protected nonsignatory, the federal policy favoring arbitration simply does not apply to him.

---

### 5. Effect of the default and litigation posture

The facts indicate Harper obtained an order of default against Davidson while he sought to compel arbitration. That posture underscores that:

- Harper elected to litigate its claims against Davidson personally, not merely to pursue Gold Reserve as the contracting party.
- Davidson’s attempt to invoke arbitration is defensive and personal; it is not Gold Reserve itself invoking the clause.

Even setting waiver issues aside, the core defect remains: Davidson has no **independent contractual entitlement** to require Harper to arbitrate with him. The default order reinforces, rather than undermines, the characterization of Davidson as a separate litigant, not the embodiment of Gold Reserve under the contract.

---

### 6. Conclusion

Under generally applicable federal and state contract principles:

- Davidson did not sign the Harper–Gold Reserve arbitration agreement;
- He is not an assignee, successor by merger, or clearly intended third‑party beneficiary;
- His alleged misconduct is **not limited to** performing Gold Reserve’s obligations as an agent, but includes independent fraud through new entities and new solicitations; and
- Harper’s claims against him can be asserted without relying on the terms of the Harper–Gold Reserve contract, making equitable estoppel inappropriate.

Because the FAA does not expand the scope of who may enforce an arbitration clause beyond what contract law supports, a court should hold that Jon Davidson cannot compel arbitration of Harper Investors’ claims against him.

Harper Investors

1. Legal framework and standard of proof  

- The Refugee Convention (as incorporated by the 1951 Convention and the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002) and Article 3 ECHR are engaged.  
- The standard of proof is the lower civil standard: whether there is a “real risk” or “reasonable degree of likelihood” of persecution/serious harm on return, not the criminal standard.  
- The burden is on Mr. Ho to establish this real risk, but the tribunal must look at the evidence “in the round”.  
- Section 8 Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004 requires certain conduct — including delay in claiming — to be taken as damaging credibility, but it is not determinative; it is one factor in the overall assessment.

2. Core elements of Mr. Ho’s claim  

Stripped to essentials, his case is:

- He was exempt from conscription because of his father’s martyr status, but this status itself became a focus of local power and corruption.  
- “Powerful local actors” (apparently linked to the military/authorities or local power networks) repeatedly demanded bribes and assaulted him.  
- He suffered physical injuries on more than one occasion, for which he obtained treatment at River Clinic and Maple District Hospital in Ho Chi Minh City.  
- He lied to hospital staff about the cause of his injuries, fearing reprisals.  
- He fears that, if returned, the same individuals (or network) will target him again, and that effective state protection is not realistically available because of local corruption.

The Secretary of State’s core counter‑position is:

- Official documents show he was exempt from military service, so there was no genuine risk of conscription; thus the claimed motive for extortion is implausible.  
- He has produced no documentary proof of bribes and did not seek any official protection.  
- He made his asylum/protection claim only after being served with deportation papers, seriously undermining credibility under s.8.  
- Vietnam has formal anti‑corruption and legal remedies; he should be treated as able to obtain state protection.

3. Assessment of credibility and evidence  

(a) Consistency of the core account  

You indicate that Mr. Ho’s “core account has remained consistent.” There is no suggestion here of him having given radically different narratives to the Home Office or the tribunal about *who* harmed him and *why*; the primary inconsistency relied upon by the Secretary of State concerns:

- The discrepancy between his account of politically‑tinged/extortion‑motivated assaults and  
- The benign causes he allegedly gave to hospital staff about how he was injured, and  
- The fact that official documents say he is exempt from conscription.

English courts and tribunals recognise that victims of violence — particularly when fearing corrupt officials or power networks — commonly conceal the true cause of injuries when speaking to local medical staff, police or other officials, precisely because they do *not* trust those systems. His explanation for lying to hospital staff (fear of retaliation) is, in principle, inherently plausible, and consistent with his broader case about local power structures.

The documentary evidence that he was exempt from military service does *not* logically negate the core of his story. His case is that corrupt actors *misused* the threat of conscription and his status as leverage; such misuse is compatible with formal exemption. That is, the presence of an official exemption can be exploited by local officials or intermediaries (“pay us so we don’t make trouble about your exemption”), and does not by itself make his account incredible.

So, the official exemption tends to undermine any suggestion that he was genuinely at risk of *lawful* conscription, but the question for asylum is whether he was subject to *unlawful* violence and extortion. On that narrower question, the exemption document has limited weight.

(b) Medical records as corroboration  

The medical reports from River Clinic and Maple District Hospital are important:

- They are contemporaneous and independent.  
- They record physical injuries of the kind expected from assaults.  

They do not, of themselves, prove *who* inflicted the harm or for what purpose, but under the low standard of proof they significantly reduce the scope for saying that his story of repeated beatings is wholly fabricated. When taken with a consistent oral account and supportive country evidence regarding violence and corruption, such medical records are typically treated as meaningful corroboration.

The Secretary of State emphasises that the records reflect a different (benign) history of the cause of injury. However:

- It is entirely consistent with both human behaviour and country evidence on corruption that a victim may fabricate a “safe” history to a local clinic.  
- Tribunals frequently accept that traumatised or fearful applicants will not give accurate histories in unsafe environments.  

So the medical evidence tends to *support* his claim that he was repeatedly injured, and his explanation for misreporting the cause of injury is not implausible.

(c) Absence of proof of bribes and of formal complaints  

Lack of receipts for bribes or proof of illegal payments is, in a context of corruption, unsurprising — bribes are typically cash, unreceipted and informal. Courts are cautious about drawing too strong an adverse inference from the absence of documentation one would not reasonably expect to exist.

Similarly, where a claimant says that the police or local authorities are part of, or beholden to, the same networks that are persecuting him, not complaining can be explicable. Case law on state protection recognises that if a claimant credibly explains why complaining would be futile or dangerous, an absence of complaint is not fatal. It is a factor, but not determinative.

On your summary, Mr. Ho has given a plausible explanation — fear of local power structures and futility of complaint — which sits coherently with country material indicating that in parts of Vietnam corruption is endemic, and official mechanisms do not function effectively in practice.

(d) Delay in claiming asylum: s.8, 2004 Act  

Mr. Ho only claimed protection after being served with a deportation notice, which is squarely within the sort of conduct that s.8 requires to be treated as damaging to credibility.

However, the appellate courts have been clear that s.8:

- Is a mandatory *factor* but not a “trump card.”  
- Does not relieve the decision‑maker of the obligation to consider all evidence in the round.  

There can be many reasons for late claims: ignorance of the asylum system, prioritising family or criminal proceedings, mistrust of authorities, or a genuine (but belated) realisation of risk on return after deportation becomes concrete.

Here, Mr. Ho’s criminal conviction obviously gives him a motive to resist deportation; that opportunistic element cannot be ignored. Nonetheless, if his account of past harm is reasonably supported and consistent, the delay—while damaging—cannot by itself justify rejecting his account as false, particularly when physical injuries are independently documented.

On balance, the delay reduces the weight to be given to his uncorroborated assertions, but the presence of corroborating medical evidence and plausible explanations mean the claim cannot be dismissed solely for that reason.

(e) Country conditions and state protection  

The Secretary of State relies on:

- The existence of anti‑corruption laws and formal remedies in Vietnam.  

Yet English case law is clear: the test is whether *effective* protection is reasonably available in practice, not merely whether a legal framework exists on paper. Where objective country material shows that:

- Local officials often act with impunity,  
- Complaints can provoke reprisals, and  
- High‑level anti‑corruption efforts do not reliably reach localities,

a tribunal can find that no “sufficiency of protection” exists for a particular individual in a particular area.

Your summary indicates that the country evidence acknowledges that “local corruption can in practice nullify formal protections and deter complaints.” If Mr. Ho’s account of being repeatedly assaulted by actors connected to local power networks is accepted even to the lower standard, it is difficult then to say that meaningful protection would be available to him in that same environment.

4. Past persecution and future risk  

(a) Past harm  

The combination of:

- Consistent narrative,

1. Statutory and doctrinal framework

– 26 U.S.C. § 2055(a) allows an estate tax deduction for transfers to charity.  
– When a trust splits interests between a noncharitable life beneficiary and a charitable remainderman, the deduction is allowed only if the charitable remainder is “presently ascertainable” and hence severable from the noncharitable interest. Treas. Reg. § 20.2055‑2(a).  
– After the 1969 changes, Congress generally denied deductions for most “split‑interest” trusts unless they are in CRAT/CRUT or similar qualified forms. § 2055(e)(2).  
– Section 2055(e)(3) is a transitional/reformation provision: if a “reformable interest” in an instrument executed before a cutoff date is judicially reformed into a qualified form, the charitable deduction can be allowed as if the instrument originally satisfied the requirements—*but only* if the statute’s predicates (including the execution date and the nature of the original interest) are satisfied.

So there are two big gates the estate must pass through:

1. The “execution date” gate: Was this a pre‑cutoff “reformable interest” within § 2055(e)(3)?  
2. The “presently ascertainable” gate: Was the remainder interest of the type the statute and regulations permit to be reformed for federal tax purposes?

If the estate loses on either, the deduction fails.

---

2. Execution date: effect of the 1982 codicil

a. Governing principle – republication by codicil

Under longstanding testamentary doctrine (followed in most states), a codicil that refers to and modifies a will “republishes” the will. The combined dispositive scheme is treated, as a matter of property law, as speaking from the date of the last codicil, unless the testator clearly provides otherwise. That is the default rule courts apply in construing wills.

Federal estate tax law routinely uses state law to determine the existence and nature of property interests. Once the state‑law interest is identified, federal law attaches the tax consequence. So when § 2055(e)(3) talks about an instrument “executed” before a certain date, the natural starting point is to ask: under state testamentary law, when was this governing instrument effectively executed (i.e., put in final, binding form)?

b. What Mary Winston did

– 1971: executed the original will and trust with Kevin Fletcher’s life interest and remainder to Elmwood.  
– 1972, 1977, 1982: executed codicils that altered the very package of benefits making up Fletcher’s life interest. These codicils did not merely change a minor bequest; they adjusted the same dispositive pattern that creates the split‑interest trust (the life interest and the charitable remainder).

By 1982, after the effective dates of the stricter split‑interest rules, Mary Winston is actively revisiting and modifying the life estate that burdens the charitable remainder.

c. Why a court should treat the instrument as executed in 1982

(i) State‑law testamentary doctrine

Under the usual rule of republication by codicil, the 1982 codicil causes the will and trust, as a single integrated dispositive scheme, to “speak” as of 1982. That is precisely how state courts determine the operative date of the governing instrument.

(ii) Statutory text and structure

The government’s argument is that § 2055(e)(3) applies only to “reformable interests” in instruments executed before the cutoff. Congress knew how to distinguish original wills from codicils. If Congress had wanted pre‑1979 wills to retain grandfather protection despite later codicils altering the same dispositive plan, it could have said so explicitly (e.g., by referring to “wills originally executed before [date], regardless of subsequent codicils”). It did not.

Instead, Congress drew the line by *execution date of the governing instrument*—which, under state law, is updated when the testator later re‑executes or republishes through a codicil affecting the dispositive scheme.

(iii) Policy and legislative purpose

The transitional, more generous treatment of pre‑cutoff instruments exists because those instruments were drafted in ignorance of the new split‑interest rules. Once a testator has revisited the dispositive scheme *after* the effective date of the new rules (as Mary did in 1982), the rationale for special grandfathering largely evaporates. The testator (and drafter) at that point can and should conform to the CRAT/CRUT or similar formats if they want a charitable deduction.

Allowing a testator in 1982 to keep relying on 1971 grandfathering, while at the same time materially changing the life interest that burdens the charity, would extend the transitional rule beyond its evident purpose.

(iv) The estate’s counter‑argument

The estate argues that because Congress removed earlier language that explicitly tied codicils to execution, “execution of the will” should mean only the original 1971 instrument. But:

– That is a thin textual hook, especially against the background of well‑settled state law that treats a will as republished on codicil.  
– It would create an arbitrary distinction where a testator can keep modifying substantive trust terms decades after the statutory cutoff and still claim to be governed by pre‑cutoff law, simply because she labels each change a “codicil.”

A court applying normal interpretive tools, and cognizant of both state testamentary doctrine and the policy of § 2055(e)(3), is more likely to adopt the government’s position: the operative governing instrument—Mary Winston’s will as modified by the 1982 codicil—is treated as executed in 1982, i.e., *after* the statutory cutoff. That alone would make the trust ineligible for the § 2055(e)(3) reformation regime.

---

3. Present ascertainability of the charitable remainder

Even if a court were to accept the estate’s preferred 1971 execution date, there is a second, independent barrier: whether the charitable remainder was “presently ascertainable” at Mary Winston’s death.

a. The legal standard

Treas. Reg. § 20.2055‑2(a) and Supreme Court case law (e.g., *Ithaca Trust Co. v. United States*, 279 U.S. 151 (1929); *Merchants Nat’l Bank v. Comm’r*, 320 U.S. 256 (1943); *Henslee v. Union Planters Nat’l Bank*, 335 U.S. 595 (1949)) require that:

– The charitable remainder be severable and its value determinable at the decedent’s death, using actuarial principles.  
– If the trustee or noncharitable beneficiary has a power or right to invade corpus not limited by an objective, enforceable standard, or subject to contingencies that cannot be reasonably quantified, then the remainder is not “presently ascertainable,” and no deduction is allowed.

In *Ithaca Trust*, the invasion power was limited to what was necessary for the widow’s “comfortable support and maintenance,” a standard long used in trust law and susceptible to actuarial estimation. In cases like *Merchants Nat’l Bank* and *Henslee*, broader standards or substantial discretion in favor of noncharitable beneficiaries made charity’s remainder too uncertain.

b. Mary Winston’s trust terms

At Mary’s death, the trustee was obligated or authorized to:

– Pay Kevin Fletcher specified monthly amounts;  
– Cover his medical expenses;  
– Pay “taxes” for him;  
– Pay “upkeep and improvements” on the Riverside residence;  
– And potentially other expenditures of a similarly broad character.

Crucially:

– These obligations are not capped by a fixed dollar limit or a formula tied to trust income;  
– “Improvements” are not limited to ordinary maintenance or preservation. On ordinary usage, they can include capital additions—adding rooms, renovating extensively, landscaping projects, or other enhancements that materially deplete corpus;  
– “Taxes” are not confined to real estate taxes on trust property. The term is broad enough to encompass income taxes on Fletcher’s outside earnings, property taxes on other assets he might own, or other tax liabilities with no relation to the trust corpus.

Thus, the trustee’s duty to expend principal for Fletcher’s benefit is open‑ended as to amount and is keyed to future decisions and contingencies (his health, his choice of improvements, his outside income and spending), not just to mortality.

c. Why the remainder is not “presently ascertainable”

The estate bears the burden to show that the charitable remainder could be valued at Mary’s death using objective standards. It cannot meet that burden here:

– The scope of “improvements” and “taxes” is not limited by an enforceable, quantifiable standard like “maintenance in the condition existing at the testatrix’s death” or “necessary expenses for preservation of the property.”  
– Instead, there is a mandated or broad power to spend principal for Fletcher’s needs and wishes that can vary wildly depending on subjective choices after Mary’s death. That is exactly the sort of open‑ended invasion power the regulations and cases treat as fatal to present ascertainability.  
– While one could attempt to impose “real world” assumptions on likely expenses, federal law does not allow the deduction to turn on speculative guesses about how extravagant the life beneficiary will be or how healthy he will remain. The uncertainty must be reduced to a reasonably definite standard enforceable in equity; otherwise the charity’s interest is too contingent.

In this respect, the case is closer to *Merchants Nat’l Bank* and *Henslee* than to *Ithaca Trust*: the noncharitable beneficiary’s rights and the trustee’s duties are too indefinite and too potentially invasive of corpus to allow reliable actuarial valuation.

Therefore, as of Mary Winston’s death, Elmwood University’s remainder was *not* “presently ascertainable.” Absent § 2055(e)(3) reformation within its carefully drawn parameters, no charitable deduction is allowable.

---

4. Effect of the 1988 state‑court reformation

Section 2055(e)(3) does provide that, if an otherwise nonqualifying split‑interest created by a pre‑cutoff instrument is judicially reformed into a qualified form (e.g., fixed annuity or unitrust interest), the remainder may become deductible and the reformation may be treated as relating back to the date of death.

But two critical limitations apply:

1. The interest must fall within the statutory definition of a “reformable interest” in a pre‑cutoff instrument. As discussed, because the will was effectively re‑executed in 1982, it is not a pre‑cutoff instrument at all.  
2. Even if timing were favorable, the original interest must fit within the class of interests Congress chose to make reformable. A trust in which the charity’s remainder was not presently ascertainable due to unlimited powers or broad mandates to invade corpus for the noncharitable beneficiary is not the paradigm Congress intended to salvage—especially when that uncertainty stems from open‑ended, non‑standardized obligations like “improvements” and global “taxes.”

Moreover, a state‑court reformation cannot by itself dictate federal tax consequences. Under *Commissioner v. Estate of Bosch*, 387 U.S. 456 (1967), federal courts look to how the state’s highest court would interpret the instrument and statute, and they apply federal tax law independently. If the federal statute does not authorize a retroactive deduction—because its conditions on timing and the nature of the interest are not met—no state decree can “manufacture” the deduction.

Here, the 1988 reformation came only after Mary’s death and, on these facts, falls outside the class of instruments Congress allowed to be retroactively cured. Thus it cannot salvage the charitable deduction.

---

5. Conclusion

Putting it all together:

– The 1982 codicil, under standard state testamentary doctrine, republishes the will and makes the governing instrument speak as of 1982. A court should therefore treat the trust as executed *after* the statutory cutoff for § 2055(e)(3) grandfathering. That alone bars use of the reformation provision.  
– Independently, the trust terms at Mary’s death gave Kevin Fletcher broad, effectively unlimited rights to expenditures from principal (medical expenses, unspecified taxes, “upkeep and improvements” to a residence) with no objective ceiling or sufficiently definite standard. Under the regulations and Supreme Court precedents, that makes Elmwood University’s remainder not “presently ascertainable,” preventing a charitable deduction as of the date of death.  
– Because the trust fails both the execution‑date requirement and the present‑ascertainability requirement for a reformable interest, the 1988 state‑court reformation cannot retroactively create a federal estate tax charitable deduction.

A US court applying § 2055(e)(3), the regulations, and relevant case law should therefore find for the Government and deny the deduction.
